title: is philly actually making money ~ or does it just look like money is moving?

body.text: i’ve been thinking about something lately that i don’t hear enough people in philly talk about.

we see money everywhere. new restaurants, new bars, sections, bottles, cars, clothes, businesses opening, events every weekend and people constantly presenting some version of success. but i keep coming back to one question: is philadelphia actually becoming wealthier, or are we just getting better at making it look like money is around?
there’s a difference between money being spent and wealth being built.

as somebody who has provided services in this city for more than a decade, i’ve had a front-row seat to seeing where money flows and where it doesn’t. there was a time when it felt like the local service economy moved differently. designers were getting paid. barbers, stylists, photographers, vendors, printers, educators, event workers and other small businesses were paying each other for services because everybody understood they couldn’t do everything themselves.

one person made money, paid somebody else for a service, that person paid somebody else, and the money continued moving through different hands. that circulation matters because a healthy economy isn’t just about somebody having money. it’s also about how many people can create value from that money before it leaves the community.
somewhere along the way, that started feeling different.

technology gave us access to tools that used to require another person. now u can build your own website, design something yourself, generate content, edit videos, automate parts of your business and learn almost anything online. that access is powerful, but it also created this mindset of, “why should i pay somebody when i can just do it myself?”
individually, that might make sense. but what happens when everybody thinks like that?
what happens when nobody hires the designer, photographer, developer, consultant or person who specializes in something because everybody is trying to become an entire company by themselves?
we can save money individually while weakening the ecosystem collectively.

i’m not against learning how to do things yourself. i actually believe people should understand the systems they depend on. but being capable doesn’t mean u should do everything alone. sometimes ownership is also understanding what deserves your attention and what another skilled person should be paid to handle.
that brings me to another question: where is the new money being created?
when i look around philly, there are certain industries that seem to continuously receive attention and spending. food. liquor. nightlife.
and those are real industries. restaurants create jobs. bars create jobs. nightlife creates economic activity. hospitality matters. i’m not saying those businesses shouldn’t exist.
i’m asking why they seem to be some of the few lanes we consistently know how to support.
food and liquor cannot be the economic ceiling for a city like philadelphia in 2026.
we can do more than another restaurant, another lounge or another club that feels like a slightly different version of the one that opened six months ago.
especially when we have generations of people who understand technology, culture, design, education, trades and entrepreneurship in ways previous generations didn’t have access to.
sometimes the opportunity isn’t opening another version of the business already making money. sometimes the opportunity is building what that business still needs.

instead of everybody trying to open another club, who is building the charging stations for the people inside of them? who is developing better reservation systems? who handles their customer data? who trains their staff? who builds their technology? who improves their operations? who develops the systems that help those businesses run better?
that’s the kind of economic thinking i want to see more of.

i want to see hair and beauty continue becoming larger companies. i want to see more trade schools, technical services, education businesses, creative agencies, software companies, business development services, financial education, youth programs and new infrastructure ideas.
i want us creating businesses around problems that actually need solving.
and i want our conversations about money to mature too.
not just “fix your credit.”

teach people what credit actually is. teach people how to use it responsibly and legally. teach people how businesses access capital. teach people the difference between revenue and profit. teach people about cash flow. teach people how assets work. teach people how ownership works.
teach people how money moves.
and more importantly, teach people how money stays.
because making money and building wealth are not the same skill.
when i say philly sometimes feels full of “paper money,” i’m not saying everybody is broke. i’m talking about the difference between visible consumption and actual ownership.
we can see somebody spend $1,000 in a section, but we can’t see their balance sheet.
we can see the car, but we don’t know how it’s financed.
we can see somebody launch a business, but we don’t know whether that business is profitable six months later.
we see the appearance of money constantly.
what i’m interested in is what’s underneath the appearance.

are households building assets? are small businesses becoming more profitable? are people hiring? are businesses surviving long enough to grow beyond the founder? are we creating companies that can employ other people? are more people becoming owners? is our collective wealth actually increasing?
those are the questions i care about.
and i’m not asking them because i think philly lacks potential.
i think the opposite.

this city has an unbelievable amount of talent. creative people, builders, tradespeople, entrepreneurs, educators, technologists and people who understand culture before the rest of the country even realizes something is becoming culture.
that’s exactly why i question what we’re doing economically.
because i don’t think our potential matches what we’re currently producing.
maybe the next chapter of philadelphia business isn’t everybody becoming more “self made.”
maybe it’s us getting better at recognizing each other’s value again.
hiring each other. building with each other. sharing knowledge. creating businesses around new problems. developing industries instead of only individual brands.
and thinking beyond what looks profitable today toward what can actually create ownership, sustainability and wealth tomorrow.
so i’ll end where i started:
is philly actually becoming wealthier ~ or does it just look like more money is moving?
and if the answer is somewhere in between, what would it take for us to turn more of that movement into something that actually lasts?
peace ~
my innerg frequency on the philadelphia economy.
